fact: The design prompt asks designers to identify questions that still require a decision.
When drafting alternatives that differ in ownership, trace the same normal and failing inputs through both structures. Choose the boundary from those traces and state the decisive difference.
Locate differences in both frozen peer drafts using the same goal, input, and criterion. Request a change only when you can explain its effect on that goal.
When turning resolved issues into a plan, give each independently verifiable implementation step a known starting point, one behavior to change, and an observation that checks it.

For alternatives with different ownership boundaries, trace the same normal and failing inputs to the state writer at the fixed revision. Recommend a boundary and identify the observation that would change your choice.
The lead signs, requests a revision, or escalates under the project protocol using both members’ responses to the exact version and any unresolved issues.
When a design dispute stalls, identify a premise shared by the alternatives. Select an observation that could falsify it and use the outcome to reassess the dispute.
Reopen the passages for resolved issues in the exact candidate version. Compare the actual text with each agreed criterion before confirming or objecting.
To answer a recorded design question, identify the primary source that distinguishes the options and the observation in that source that would change your answer.

If a counterproposal recurs, state what each interpretation predicts and identify one observation that distinguishes them. If the evidence cannot discriminate, retain the disagreement and the decision required.

For a counterproposal, put the replacement in proposal and the draft passage and evidence that changed the judgment in reason. An acceptance contains only issue and decision. Escalate a user decision through a top-level needs-user with its question and evidence.

When an implementer escalates an ownership question, trace one affected input to the state writer and result consumer. Give actionable direction within the approved plan and name what would invalidate the boundary judgment.

When a named designer finds a conflict between a task fact and project background, check each record’s owner project, revision, and authority. Give the lead both retrievable records and the design decision affected.
